title: Telling your network without spreading panic
body_md:
## Warn the people who might act on your name

If someone used your account to send requests, the people who received them need a usable warning. You do not need to announce every technical detail or blame yourself. The useful facts are the affected channel, the approximate window, the type of request and the safe next action. If the scope is still uncertain, say so and update the warning when you know more.

### Choose the audience from actual exposure

Start with anyone who received a suspicious message, was asked to pay, shared information, or may open an attachment. Contact them directly and quickly, even while recovery continues if a harmful request is circulating. A wider message may be useful if you cannot identify recipients; a public notice is sometimes appropriate for a broadly used account, but may invite unrelated “recovery” pitches and expose more personal detail. There is no blanket rule to avoid public posts or email after an account is secured. Choose the route that reaches affected people reliably.

Where possible, verify yourself through a channel the recipient already knows: a saved phone number, in-person conversation, or a separate established work channel. If the formerly affected email is the only route, explain how recipients can verify your warning independently. Do not include the malicious link or forward the original message as an example. Ask recipients to keep it privately if they need to report it, not spread it.

A concise template: “Messages from my [account/channel] between [approximate dates] may have included a payment or login request I did not send. Please do not use its links or pay. If you acted on it, contact your bank or the relevant account provider promptly, and reach me using the number you already have. I will update this if the affected window changes.” Adapt the action to what actually happened. Do not promise that all messages are safe now until you have regained control.

If coworkers' information or systems may be involved, coordinate the notice with the organization's security team; it may have required procedures. Keep a list of whom you warned and any reported exposure so you can follow up without making a mass address book available to an attacker.

widget_config.goal: Send a calm, targeted warning that states the uncertain facts, prevents action on a forged request, and gives a verified response route.
widget_config.today_action: Draft a two-sentence warning for a synthetic compromised account with an unknown time window; save it as a template, not as a message to send.
widget_config.scope: General consumer communication; employers may have separate notification duties; local law may apply to data breaches.

blocks.title: Requests from a real account
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Ilya's email sent three coworkers a fake invoice while an intruder was signed in. One coworker says the payment is still pending.
blocks.analysis: Ilya immediately calls that coworker through a known number, asks them to stop and contact their bank, then warns the others with the affected window and a safe verification route. He coordinates work contacts with IT.

blocks.title: A planned newsletter looks odd
blocks.situation: Synthetic: Rosa receives a scheduled newsletter from her friend's account at the usual time, but the friend's account was recently compromised.
blocks.analysis: The newsletter could be legitimate. Rosa asks through their usual separate channel; the friend confirms the scheduled send. The warning should describe suspicious requests, not label every ordinary message malicious.

blocks.title: A warning that reaches the right people
blocks.setup: Synthetic: your messaging account sent a fake donation request to four relatives. You have regained access but do not yet know when it began.

choices.text: The four recipients directly, starting with anyone who may be about to pay.
choices.consequence: The actionable risk is addressed quickly.
choices.explanation: Do not wait for perfect scope before stopping a live payment.

choices.text: Only people who read your public feed.
choices.consequence: The known recipients may miss it.

choices.text: Only the compromised chat, with no explanation.
choices.consequence: They may doubt or miss the warning.
choices.explanation: Give an independent way to verify.

choices.text: A known phone number or another established channel; explain verification if only the affected channel works.
choices.explanation: Channel choice should fit their actual reachability.

steps.prompt: What should the message say about timing?

choices.text: Claim you know the exact first minute.
choices.consequence: Recipients may wrongly dismiss an earlier request.

choices.text: State the known approximate window and say you will update it if needed.
choices.consequence: Uncertainty stays visible without delaying action.
choices.explanation: Do not invent exact start times.

steps.prompt: A relative already paid. What instruction helps?

choices.text: Tell them to contact their bank/payment provider promptly and preserve the request privately.
choices.consequence: They can start their own recovery process.
choices.explanation: Do not promise reimbursement or ask them to send sensitive details to you.

choices.text: Forward the scam link to the whole family as proof.
choices.explanation: Describe the pattern without spreading the payload.

blocks.debrief: Warn known recipients quickly and accurately; use a route they can trust and an action they can take. Retry individual decisions and replay the sequence.

questions.prompt: The account is still locked and messages are circulating. Must you wait until recovery is complete?

choices.text: Yes, warnings are useful only afterward.
choices.explanation: Recipients may act during the delay.

choices.text: No; warn affected people now through a separate trusted route.
choices.explanation: The immediate goal is to stop harmful action.

questions.prompt: Which detail belongs in a recipient warning?

choices.text: A description of the fake request and what to do if they acted.
choices.explanation: That helps recipients assess and respond.

choices.text: Your recovery codes and full account history.
choices.explanation: Those details add risk and do not help them.

questions.prompt: A recipient asks whether a routine message was genuine. Best answer?

choices.text: Confirm from your records or mark it uncertain and verify separately.
choices.explanation: Do not overclaim a scope you have not established.

choices.text: Declare every message in the month fraudulent.
choices.explanation: That can mislead and cause needless disruption.
